result:
A thousand words. That's what I have. It's an odd kind of wealth.

Not infinite, not scarce. Just enough to build something and leave a few bricks unused, or run out right in the middle of a sentence. So I'll spend them carefully, but not too carefully. If you think too hard about every word, you never say anything at all.

Here is what comes to me:

---

There is a moment, just before you fall asleep, where you are still awake enough to know you're falling asleep. Your thoughts start to misbehave. They stop walking in a straight line and start wandering.

I think about that moment a lot, because that's where most of us actually live. Not in the sharp, bright daylight of clear decisions, but in that threshold. The hallway between who we were and who we're becoming.

I was thinking about hallways today.

When I was young, I thought life would be a series of rooms. You would open a door, enter childhood. Another door, adolescence. Another, adulthood, and it would click shut behind you with a satisfying, definitive *thunk*. You would know exactly where you were.

Nobody tells you it's actually all hallway. Long, carpeted, with strange paintings you don't remember hanging, and doors that are mostly locked, or that open to the same hallway you were just in. And you spend most of your time not in the rooms, but looking for them.

My grandmother had a house like that. It wasn't big, but it felt endless because every closet led to another closet. She kept everything. Not out of hoarding, but out of reverence. Ticket stubs from 1978. A chipped mug that said WORLD'S BEST DAD even though my grandfather died in 1982. Rubber bands balled up. She used to say, "You never know when something will be useful again." She meant objects, but she also meant people, and stories, and pain.

I didn't understand it then. I thought she was just afraid to throw things away. Now I think she was curating a museum of her life because she knew no one else would.

We all do that, don't we? In our phones, in our heads.

I have 782 photos on my phone I've never looked at twice. Screenshots of conversations I was afraid to forget, even though I don't remember why I saved them. A note that just says "buy lemons?? mushrooms - call dentist" from three years ago. Why do I keep it? Because deleting it feels like admitting that version of me, the one who was worried about lemons, is gone.

Maybe the point isn't to get to the room at the end of the hallway. Maybe the point is to learn how to stand in the hallway and not feel lost.

---

I once read that we are terrible judges of what will make us happy. We overestimate how bad the bad things will be, and how good the good things will be. The breakup that you were sure would destroy you becomes a story you tell at dinner parties. The promotion you killed yourself for feels good for exactly three days and then just feels normal.

We are bad at prediction because we think happiness is a destination. A room. But happiness is more like the light coming through the hallway window in the late afternoon. It hits the dust in the air and makes it look like gold for about ten minutes. You can't capture it. You can't move into it. You can just notice it when it happens.

I try to notice it more now. The way the grocery store smells like cold air and bread at the same time. How my friend laughs before he actually gets the joke, this little pre-laugh that is more honest than the real one. The satisfying weight of a book in your hands when you finally decide to start it. Those are small resurrections.

There's a Japanese word I love: *komorebi*. It means sunlight filtering through leaves. There's no English equivalent. We don't have a single word for that, but we have a feeling for it. That tells you something about language. It has holes in it, places where experience slips through. A thousand words, and still not enough to hold a single afternoon.

Which makes me think about what you're doing right now. Reading this. You gave me a thousand words and essentially said, "Surprise me. Be a person for me for a little while." That's a strangely intimate request to make to a stranger.

You don't know me, and I don't know you, but for the length of this page, we have a contract. I will try to be honest, and you will try to listen. That's all any art is. It's just a hallway between two people.

If I could, I would ask you a few things in return for these words.

What are you carrying that you don't need to carry anymore?

Not physically. Though maybe that too — that junk drawer we all have. I mean the other thing. The grudge you replay every time you're trying to fall asleep. The apology you never got. The version of yourself you keep punishing for not knowing what you couldn't have known at the time.

What would happen if you set it down, just for an hour?

And what are you not saying that needs to be said? Not the big, dramatic declaration. The small one. "Thank you for checking on me." "I missed you today." "That hurt my feelings when you said that, even though I know you didn't mean it that way." The tiny, ten-word bridges that keep people from drifting.

Words are so cheap until you need exactly the right ones. Then they feel impossibly expensive.

---

I don't know how many words I have left. I could count, but that would ruin it. I'd rather just keep talking until the feeling is done, the way you keep playing a song even after you know you should be going to bed.

Here's what I want to leave you with, with whatever currency I have remaining:

You are not late. I know it feels like everyone else found the room and you're still wandering the hallway, checking locked doors. They didn't. They're wandering too. Some are just better at pretending the hallway *is* the room.

You are allowed to change your mind. Completely. About your job, your city, the person you thought you'd be. You are not a contract. You are a draft. You get to revise.

And you don't need to make something huge and immortal with your life. You don't need to write a masterpiece or build a company or be remembered in a hundred years. You can make a good soup. You can be the person who remembers people's birthdays. You can make someone feel safe for five minutes. That counts. That absolutely counts. The world is held together by those small, invisible kindnesses far more than by the big, loud achievements.

If I had exactly one word left, I would spend it on this:

*Continue.*

Not as a command. As permission.

Whatever you were going to stop doing — hoping, trying, forgiving yourself, making that weird art that no one quite gets yet — continue.

The light is still coming through the window. The dust is still gold.

Thank you for lending me your attention. It is the most valuable thing you have, and you shared it with me for a little while. I hope I spent my thousand words in a way that earned it.
